synopsis: Synchronization is a prerequisite for reconstructing scenes, replaying recordings and assessing braking performance, but the existing warning system's retention of synchronized raw data and useful labels is not established [f3852, f5232, f1139, f519]. Recordings should preserve hardware timestamps on a common clock, calibration, clock offsets, synchronization status, dropped-data counters and resynchronization events; per-frame timestamps may be insufficient for moving machines with rolling or scanning sensors [f5629, f4016, f4018]. Unsynchronized clocks can create an entirely artificial algorithm latency of 100–300 ms, while smaller errors can reorder approach events; at 15 km/h, a 100 ms timing error shifts measured object position by 42 cm [f5654, f5655, f12738]. The booklet identifies timing and cross-sensor consistency as gaps in its seven sensor questions: realistic individual sensor values do not establish correct fused perception or braking when acquisition, network, controller or actuator timing is wrong [f5092, f5101]. Recommended validation includes known-event tests timestamping every stage from detection to measurable deceleration, independently calibrated and synchronized ground truth, and a dedicated data-pedigree workstream [f6159, f5642, f11244, f10346]. Tool integration must align clocks, time bases, dynamics and rendered sensor poses while preserving deterministic ECU replay; ASAM MDF 4.3.0, dated September 2025, provides a standardized recording format that includes synchronization metadata [f8718, f8721, f7115].
